title: Virtual reality as a tool for cognitive and sensory modulation
summary: Virtual Reality (VR) has emerged as a transformative medium in neuroscience, moving beyond entertainment into a robust tool for experimental manipulation. Traditionally, studying cognitive and sensory processes required a trade-off between controlled laboratory settings and real-world ecological validity. VR bridges this gap by providing immersive, three-dimensional environments that can be precisely modulated to isolate specific neural responses. By engaging multiple sensory modalities—visual, auditory, and increasingly somatosensory—VR creates a sense of "presence" that activates the brain in ways traditional 2D stimuli cannot. This immersive capacity allows researchers to investigate how the human brain processes complex sensory inputs and orchestrates cognitive functions in real-time.

title: Current Perspectives of The Neurobiology of Prosody and Rhythm
summary: Prosody and rhythm are core components of speech that allow the brain to transform acoustic signals into linguistic and affective meaning. The interplay of pitch, stress, timing, and intonation patterns conveys syntactic structure, emotion, and communicative intent, while rhythmic organization supports segmentation, prediction, and motor coordination. Recent neuroscience research has revealed that prosodic and rhythmic functions depend on distributed neural networks spanning auditory, motor, subcortical, and cerebellar regions, coordinated by oscillatory activity across temporal scales. Despite these advances, key questions remain about how these systems develop, how their dysfunction contributes to communication disorders, and how prosody interacts with music, movement, and emotion across contexts and languages. Bridging these knowledge gaps is essential to understand how the brain encodes the temporal and melodic contours that shape human speech.

summary: Predictive Coding (PC) is a prominent theoretical framework that posits that a core function of the brain is a hierarchical inference process. It actively generates predictions about the causes of sensory input and continuously updates these based on "prediction errors" (the mismatch between expectation and reality). This parsimonious model offers a mechanistic account for a wide range of typical cognitive functions, from basic sensory inference and perceptual stability to motor control and decision-making.

summary: The Central Nervous System (CNS) provides information about how individuals collect information from their surroundings, how they process that information to make decisions, and finally, how they behave and act in their environment. CNS information can be gathered from three main sources: (1) electrical currents (e.g., electroencephalography – EEG) or electrocorticography (ECoG)), (2) magnetic fields (e.g., magnetoencephalography – MEG), and (3) level of blood oxygen or blood flow (e.g., functional near infrared spectroscopy – NIRS or functional magnetic resonance imaging – fMRI). This neuroinformation is being decoded to develop neural interfaces that aim to establish, re-establish and/or improve the neural interconnectivity of CNS in order to optimize the human-environment interaction. Not only decoding of neuroinformation has been pursued so far, but also finding the best way to recode neuroinformation by brain stimulation has been of interest in the scientific community.

title: Interactions between the nervous, immune, and endocrine systems in brain health
summary: Brain health is the result of intricate communication between the nervous, immune, and endocrine systems. Traditionally, these systems were studied in isolation; however, recent advances highlight their dynamic crosstalk and their collective influence on brain function. Neuroinflammation, hormonal signaling, and immune responses are now recognized as critical factors in neurological development, homeostasis, and disease. Disruptions in these inter-system interactions are implicated in a myriad of conditions, such as neurodegenerative diseases, psychiatric disorders, and metabolic syndromes. As our understanding deepens, there is a growing appreciation for integrative approaches that examine these systems together, offering novel insights into mechanisms underlying brain health and disease.

title: Predictive motor control and internal models
summary: Skilled motor behaviour relies on the central nervous system’s capacity to predict, rather than merely react to, the sensory consequences of its own actions. From reaching for a cup of coffee to maintaining balance on a moving train, every voluntary movement relies on the central nervous system’s ability to anticipate the sensory consequences of its own actions. This predictive capacity is thought to be supported by internal models: neural representations of the body and the external world that allow the brain to estimate forthcoming states and select appropriate motor commands. Forward models predict the sensory outcomes of motor actions, while inverse models compute the motor commands required to achieve a desired sensory or kinematic goal. Together, they form the computational backbone of skilled, flexible, and adaptive behaviour, and their disruption is increasingly recognised as a hallmark of several neurological and psychiatric conditions.

Neuroactive microbial metabolites and human brain function: mechanisms, biomarkers, and clinical implications
summary: In the rapidly evolving field of neurogastroenterology, mounting evidence highlights the profound influence of neuroactive microbial metabolites on human brain function. The gut-brain axis has become a focal point for understanding how metabolites produced by gut microbiota, reshaped by factors such as diet, medications, and stress, interact with the central nervous system. Recent studies have delineated pathways by which short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan metabolites, bile acids, and other molecules alter blood–brain barrier integrity, microglial activation, neurotransmitter systems, and neural connectivity. Despite promising insights, critical questions remain regarding the reproducibility of findings, individual susceptibility, and translation to clinical practice. There remains a significant gap in mapping specific metabolite signatures to neuropsychiatric phenotypes, as well as understanding how genetic and environmental factors modulate these effects.

title: Restoring Sensation and Perception: From neural coding to adaptive neurotechnology
summary: Sensation and perception arise from complex neural processes through which the human brain encodes, integrates, interprets, and adapts to information from the external environment and the body. Disruption of these processes can result from sensory loss, stroke, traumatic brain injury, spinal cord injury, neurodegenerative disorders, chronic pain, and other neurological conditions, substantially impairing communication, mobility, independence, and quality of life. At the same time, rapid advances in neural recording, computational modelling, brain–computer interfaces, neuroprosthetics, artificial intelligence, and adaptive neuromodulation are creating new opportunities to restore, substitute, or rehabilitate sensory and perceptual functions.

Translating Desire – Psychology, Arts, and the Neuroscience of Pleasure
summary: Subjectively and phenomenologically, sexual arousal is a state of pleasure, joy, passion, and bodily excitement, followed by delight, positive exhaustion, and relaxation. Biologically, it involves changes in physiological arousal, the release of hormones and neurotransmitters in the autonomic nervous system and the central nervous system. In dimensional biological emotion theories, it represents the highly positive endpoint in the affective space defined by valence and physiological arousal, triggered by internal or external pleasurable and erotic stimuli. From an evolutionary perspective, the purpose of sexual arousal and pleasure is to prime action disposition for approach or avoidance, thereby supporting survival and driving perceptual, cognitive, and emotional resources through motivational systems that prioritize mating and influence decision-making about sexual behaviors.

summary: Battery capacity, recharge logistics, and computational budgets are now the primary bottlenecks for scaling multi robot systems from short demos to dependable, 24/7 operations. Long horizon missions—warehousing, inspection, agriculture, environmental monitoring, and public safety—require fleets to coordinate tasks, routes, and recharge events while accounting for battery aging, stochastic demand, uncertain travel times, and heterogeneous platforms. Classical planning or perception advances alone are insufficient: persistence hinges on resource models, predictive energy usage, and infrastructure aware scheduling that closes the loop between algorithms, chargers, and the physical environment. This Research Topic focuses on the algorithmic and systems foundations that make multi robot autonomy sustainable and economically viable over days to months, emphasizing measurable mission availability, throughput, safety under energy constraints, and total cost of ownership.

Affective Computing Meets Embodied Intelligence: Emotion Perception, Reasoning, and Interaction in Embodied Agents
summary: Affective computing aims to endow machines with the ability to recognize, interpret, and respond to human emotions, while embodied intelligence emphasizes that cognition emerges through an agent's physical interaction with its environment. Historically, these two fields have advanced along largely separate trajectories: affective computing has focused on emotion recognition from facial, vocal, physiological, and textual signals, whereas embodied intelligence has concentrated on perception, control, and manipulation in the physical world. Recent breakthroughs in large multimodal models, foundation models for robotics, and human-robot interaction have created unprecedented opportunities to unify the two. Emotion is no longer treated as a passive signal to be classified, but as an active component that shapes how embodied agents perceive, reason, decide, and act within dynamic, socially rich environments.

title: Cognitive–motor interactions in aging: neural mechanisms, behavioral signatures, and functional consequences
summary: The fields of motor control and cognitive psychology have been traditionally separate, but research has fundamentally reshaped this distinction. We now understand that motor control and cognitive functions are inextricably linked, sharing neural pathways and competing for limited resources, especially in aging. As neural efficiency declines in aging, there is a tradeoff between using resources to support motor performance and cognitive function. For example, older adults often display reduced performance on complex tasks due to cognitive-motor interference, compared to younger adults. Understanding the mechanisms behind this shift is critical for distinguishing between healthy aging and early-stage neurodegeneration. It will also facilitate the development of interventions aimed at preserving functional independence.

summary: Motor circuit disorders represent a heterogeneous group of neurological conditions characterised by disruptions in the neural pathways governing voluntary and involuntary movement. Sensory-motor integration in human movement
summary: For desired and coordinated movements, the central nervous system integrates multiple sensory feedback with motor commands. Optimum integration of multi-sensory signals from visual, vestibular, and somatosensory systems is vital to performing activities of daily life and is commonly compromised due to aging, neuromuscular disorders, and traumatic injuries. Compromised sensor-motor integration can potentially lead to a stability control deficiency, increased risk of falling, tremors, rigidity, and decreased hand dexterity, just to name a few. However, there is a limited understanding of the mechanisms responsible for sensory-motor integration, specifically, how the central nervous system adapts to changes in environmental conditions (e.g., visual input is obstructed), physical and mental health, and cognitive status. A comprehensive study of sensory-motor integration can be beneficial to healthcare professionals, neuroscientists, and human health in general.

title: Transforming Genitourinary Surgery Through Advanced Robotic Systems
summary: The field of genitourinary (GU) surgery has undergone a transformative shift with the integration of robotic technology, which now serves as a cornerstone for minimally invasive procedures. Over recent decades, advancements have evolved from pioneering platforms like PUMA 560 and Probot to current industry standards, exemplified by the da Vinci system. Robotic approaches have been lauded for improved dexterity, enhanced visualization, and better ergonomics for surgeons, leading to increasing adoption. Despite their technical promise, clinical debates remain around appropriate patient selection, comparative benefits over other minimally invasive modalities, and the economic implications of broader deployment. Although early evidence points to advantages such as reduced blood loss and faster recovery, critical gaps persist, including inconsistent outcome definitions, limited long-term data, and a lack of standardized benchmarks for both clinical and technical success.
image_alt: Transforming Genitourinary Surgery Through Advanced Robotic Systems

title: Effort, Attention, and Arousal: Brain–Body Mechanisms for Performance in the Real World
summary: Sustained performance in high-stakes, real-world environments places extraordinary demands on the human brain and body. Effort, attention, and arousal are three tightly interwoven constructs that together govern how individuals mobilize cognitive and physiological resources to meet these demands. Nowhere is this more critical than in contexts in which humans are expected to perform in high stakes environments. For example, military personnel, first responders, and individuals of the like must maintain peak cognitive performance under conditions of extreme stress, fatigue, sensory overload, and physical exertion. Despite decades of laboratory research, the neural and peripheral mechanisms underpinning the interaction between mental effort, attentional control, and arousal remain incompletely understood — particularly in the demanding and ecologically complex environments that are present in real-world scenarios.

summary: Recent advances in Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), particularly large language models (LLMs), have transformed how machines interpret, reason, and communicate. At the same time, robotics research has made significant progress in edge computing, sensor fusion, and real-time perception systems, enabling deployment in dynamic and resource-constrained environments. Despite these developments, a critical gap remains in the integration of generative AI with embodied robotic systems operating at the edge, especially in wearable robotics such as smart helmets, assistive devices, and human-augmentation systems. Current research topics emphasise either cloud-based intelligence or isolated edge AI solutions, but lack a unified framework for real-time, context-aware decision support that combines perception, reasoning, and action under strict computational constraints.

Medical robots are now increasingly utilized in various applications, such as assistant robots for tasks like sterilization, patient monitoring, and medical imaging; rehabilitation systems, including exoskeletons and smart prosthetics; as well as procedural robots deployed in surgeries and minimally invasive interventions. While these technologies often offer redundant degrees of freedom, enhancing their flexibility and dexterity in constrained environments, they also present notable challenges in kinematics, control, and real-time decision-making. summary: Traditional neuromodulation techniques, such as transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) or transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), have revolutionized our ability to non-invasively probe and alter brain activity. However, single-modality approaches often face inherent limitations in achieving highly specific or sustained effects due to the brain's distributed nature and compensatory mechanisms. A new frontier is emerging at the intersection of various stimulation methods and sensory inputs: multimodal stimulation. By combining distinct neurostimulation techniques (e.g., electrical, magnetic, optical, acoustic) with or across various sensory domains (e.g., visual, auditory, somatosensory), we can potentially unlock more sophisticated and targeted modulation of neural circuits, leading to enhanced understanding of brain function and more effective therapeutic interventions.

summary: Working memory plays a central role in the cognitive and neural systems that support speech and language acquisition. It sustains transient representations of sounds, words, and syntactic structures, allowing learners to form stable linguistic knowledge while supporting the online processing of linguistic information during comprehension and production. title: Bioactive phytochemicals with neuroimmunopharmacological properties
summary: Plants constitute a vast and still incompletely characterized reservoir of biologically active compounds. Among them are highly potent therapeutic agents such as paclitaxel, employed in oncology, and morphine, a cornerstone of severe pain management. Moreover, numerous plant-derived products contain complex phytochemical compositions that contribute to the maintenance of physiological homeostasis and may play a preventive role in the early stages of disease development. Accordingly, plant-derived substances – including crude extracts, enriched fractions, or isolated compounds – may be considered as valuable candidates for the development of therapeutics, dietary supplements, or functional food components. In any case, these substances exert measurable biological effects by modulating physiological functioning and molecular pathways.

summary: Robotic manipulation is a dynamic field at the forefront of automation and artificial intelligence. A notable limitation is the ability to perform contact-rich, fine-grained, and high-precision manipulation, crucial for real-world applications. Recent studies highlight a need for learning-based approaches, multimodal perception, and hierarchical planning strategies to overcome these barriers, aiming to improve dexterity and autonomous capabilities. Progressive efforts in the field have seen the rise of foundation models and visual-language-action models that integrate perception and action, allowing for nuanced manipulation tasks.

summary: Early definitions of interoception described it as sensing internal bodily states and distinguished it from exteroception. summary: Recent advances in visual and auditory technologies have significantly enhanced user performance and experience in Virtual Reality (VR). While haptic feedback is known to shape perception, cognition, and motor control during virtual interaction, the field is still developing principled approaches for delivering effective touch sensations using simple, adaptable, and context-aware solutions. summary: In recent years, reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated great potential in robotic tasks such as perception, control, and autonomous decision-making, becoming a key driver of robotics and embodied intelligence. However, deploying reinforcement learning policies from simulation to the real world (sim-to-real) often requires extensive hyperparameter tuning to accommodate varying tasks and dynamic environmental conditions. As robots gradually transition from controlled laboratory settings to open, dynamic real-world environments, they are increasingly confronted with challenges such as perceptual noise, environmental disturbances, and model discrepancies. These factors significantly limit the generalization and robustness of current RL methods. Therefore, improving the robustness of reinforcement learning algorithms in robot systems has become a key issue that urgently needs to be addressed.

Improving Vision-Guided Robotic Systems Through Next-Generation Hand-Eye Calibration Techniques
summary: Robotic vision systems form the foundation of modern industrial automation, enabling high-precision tasks such as assembly, inspection, and object manipulation. Central to their performance is hand-eye calibration, which defines the spatial relationship between the robotic manipulator and the visual sensor. Traditional calibration methods typically rely on multiple feature points, complex mathematical transformations, and iterative optimizations, increasing the risk of cumulative errors and computational inefficiencies. Recent approaches leveraging simplified configurations—such as single fixed feature point methods and algorithms like Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and Levenberg-Marquardt (LM)—have shown promise in reducing setup complexity. However, persistent issues with accuracy, robustness to sensor noise, and adaptability to dynamic environments highlight the need for innovative solutions that balance precision with operational efficiency.

summary: Sleep is not merely a passive state but a dynamic process fundamental to learning, memory consolidation, and cognitive performance. During sleep, the brain undergoes remarkable transformations—reorganizing neural circuits, strengthening newly acquired memories, and clearing metabolic waste accumulated during wakefulness. Decades of research have established that adequate sleep enhances learning capacity, improves problem-solving, and optimizes performance across academic, athletic, and professional domains. Conversely, sleep deprivation impairs attention, working memory, and executive function. Yet the precise multimodal mechanisms linking sleep architecture, electrophysiological activity, neurochemical processes, and behavioral outcomes remain incompletely understood. Recent advances in polysomnography, neuroimaging, electrophysiology, computational modeling, and biomarker assessment have enabled more sophisticated investigation of sleep-dependent learning and performance. title: Timing the senses: From auditory temporal coherence to audiovisual integration
summary: Human perception operates within a chaotic sensory environment, where the brain must constantly determine which signals arise from the same source. A critical mechanism for this is temporal coherence, being the degree to which different sensory features fluctuate together over time. In the auditory domain, temporal coherence is a primary driver for stream segregation, allowing the brain to bind diverse frequencies into a single "object." However, this principle extends beyond audition. Temporal structure serves as a fundamental organizing principle for perception across sensory modalities, acting as a "glue" that helps the brain determine which signals belong together. While we understand that timing is important for both auditory grouping and multisensory binding, the precise transition from intramodal temporal coherence to intermodal audiovisual integration remains a complex challenge in human neuroscience.

Modularity in Motor Control: from neural networks to muscle synergies
summary: The field of motor control is characterized by a vast array of complex behaviors that are essential for numerous daily activities. Recent research has advanced our understanding of these behaviors by breaking down the motor system into modules, examining the interplay between neurons, muscles, and brain networks. This modular approach has illuminated how different levels of the nervous system, from spinal cord circuits to extensive brain networks, collaborate to produce efficient and adaptable motor outputs. Nonetheless, significant gaps remain in our understanding of how these modules are altered in aging or neurological conditions, particularly how these changes affect motor control and the potential benefits of therapeutic interventions.

title: Neural Circuits and Network Dysfunctions in Depression and Anxiety
summary: Within human neuroscience, recent advances have transformed our perspective on depression and anxiety, reframing them as conditions of network-level dysfunction rather than isolated regional brain disturbances. Substantial evidence now implicates large-scale brain circuits supporting threat anticipation, reward processing, salience detection, cognitive control, and social-affective behaviors as core substrates underlying these disorders. While pioneering neuroimaging, genetic, and computational studies have identified distinct connectivity alterations and disrupted dynamics across these networks, key questions remain. The field is grappling with how these dysfunctions interact transdiagnostically, predict clinical heterogeneity, or evolve across the lifespan. Importantly, the translation of these circuit-based insights into diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic tools is an urgent, ongoing challenge.

title: Quantum theory, biological organization, and the mind-brain problem
summary: The relationship between physical theory and biological organization remains one of the most challenging in contemporary science. Part of the inspiration of this topic comes from the intellectual legacy of Erwin Schrödinger, especially the questions raised in What is Life? and Mind and Matter, as well as from the centenary of wave mechanics. Schrödinger’s reflections helped shape enduring discussions on order, information, stability, and the organization of living matter. Today, these themes continue to resonate in debates on biological information, neural complexity, memory, brain dynamics, and the conceptual relation between mind and brain. Rather than treating these questions as purely historical, this Research Topic approaches them as still-active problems at the intersection of theoretical physics, life sciences, and neuroscience.

title: Neural control of locomotion in daily life: Gait variability, stability, and adaptability
summary: Locomotion is one of the most fundamental relevant motor behaviours in humans. Walking in daily life is rarely the steady, cyclical activity often examined in laboratory settings; rather, it requires continuous adjustments to varying terrains, environmental demands, cognitive loads, and concurrent tasks. The neural control of locomotion therefore involves a distributed network spanning spinal central pattern generators, brainstem locomotor regions, the cerebellum, the basal ganglia, and cortical areas, all of which interact dynamically with sensory feedback to produce gait patterns that are simultaneously stable, variable, and adaptable. title: New Perspectives on the Role of Sensory Feedback in Speech Production: Volume IV
summary: Speaking represents one of our most complex motor behaviors, one that is vital to our ability to communicate. To understand how speech is produced, one crucially important question to address is: how is sensory feedback used in the speech production process? Answering this question is an important step to understanding how the motor skill of speaking is initially learned and then maintained, as numerous studies have shown that sensory feedback plays a key role in these learning processes. There is also evidence that sensory feedback is important for successful moment-by-moment control of ongoing speech output. It is natural, therefore, that significant portions of current models of speech production are devoted to explaining the role of sensory feedback. Furthermore, abnormal processing of sensory feedback appears to be involved in many disorders of speech and voice production, like laryngeal dystonia and stuttering.

title: The interplay between attention and language
summary: The capacities of awareness, selection, and sustained attention are critical for human communication, from an adult perceiving speech sounds and comprehending complex discourse, to an infant babbling surrounding speech sounds and associating new words with their meanings. When the brain is functioning atypically, due to developmental differences or an injury, the demands of linguistic processing can heavily tax attentional resources. A growing body of research highlights that deficits in one domain frequently co-occur with, and profoundly influence, impairments in the other. Understanding this dynamic interplay is important for advancing our theoretical models of typical human speech and language, and for developing more effective diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for a wide range of developmental and acquired speech and language disorders.

Beyond the Average Brain: Person-Specific Mechanisms and Within-Person Prediction
summary: Traditional neuroscience research has relied on group-level analyses, identifying average patterns across populations. However, substantial heterogeneity exists in brain structure, function, connectivity, and neurobiology across individuals. This variability is not merely noise but reflects meaningful differences in genetics, development, experience, and biology that shape cognition and behavior. Person-specific (idiographic) approaches and within-person prediction models recognize that individuals follow unique neural trajectories and respond differently to interventions. Recent advances in computational modeling, machine learning, intensive longitudinal designs, and single-subject neuroimaging enable detailed characterization of individual brain patterns and their behavioral correlates. Precision neuroscience—tailored to the individual—promises more accurate prediction, more effective interventions, and deeper mechanistic understanding of brain-behavior relationships.

title: Translational brain imaging–guided neuromodulation
summary: The intersection of advanced neuroimaging and neuromodulation is reshaping how we understand and treat disorders of the nervous system. Techniques such as transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), deep brain stimulation (DBS), and focused ultrasound have matured considerably over the past two decades. Yet their clinical impact has remained constrained by a fundamental gap: stimulation protocols are rarely informed by the individual’s brain structure and function. Neuroimaging is poised to close that gap. title: Push the System: Stimulation, Pharmacology, and Closed-Loop Tests of Cognitive Mechanisms
summary: Cognitive processes such as attention, perception, memory, executive function, and social cognition emerge from dynamic interactions between distributed neural systems. While correlational methods like neuroimaging and electrophysiology have mapped these networks extensively, they cannot establish whether a given neural signature is necessary or sufficient for a cognitive function. Causal interventions—including non-invasive brain stimulation (TMS, tDCS, tACS), pharmacological manipulation, and closed-loop neurofeedback systems—offer a powerful complement, allowing researchers to directly perturb neural systems and observe the behavioral consequences. Advances in real-time signal processing and adaptive stimulation now make it possible to test cognitive theories with unprecedented precision and mechanistic specificity.

Decoding these signals with sufficient precision to advance our understanding of neural function and to translate that understanding into clinical tools, represents one of the defining challenges of modern neuroscience. Conventional signal processing approaches, while foundational, are increasingly insufficient in the face of data complexity, inter-subject variability, and the subtlety of neural dynamics that underlie cognition, perception, and disease.

summary: Neuropsychiatric research increasingly recognizes neuroinflammation as a critical mechanism underlying psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, and first-episode psychosis. Evidence from genetics, transcriptomics, neuroimaging, and peripheral immune profiling highlights the involvement of immune-related processes, particularly microglial activation, cytokine imbalance, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, and aberrant complement-mediated synaptic pruning, in shaping disease onset, cognitive impairment, and treatment resistance. These findings suggest that immune dysregulation is not merely a secondary phenomenon but a driving factor in illness progression. However, despite the surge of recent discoveries, the exact temporal dynamics, causal mechanisms, and the translational potential of immune signals remain incompletely understood. Research efforts integrating human anatomy, functional neuroanatomy, and cellular neuroscience, including studies of vertebrate models, have been pivotal in revealing the intricate organization of basal ganglia circuits. In particular, dopaminergic neurons are crucial modulators within these networks, influencing processes ranging from nervous system development to the plasticity underlying learning and adaptation. Dysfunction of these circuits is implicated in various neurological and psychiatric conditions, emphasizing the importance of understanding their anatomy and physiology across different species and developmental stages.

title: Multidisciplinary perspectives on the processing of focus in human communication
summary: Focus, the grammatical means of highlighting information to convey meaning and intention, is a fundamental component of human communication, critical not only for oral interaction but also for advancing natural human-machine interfaces. Cross-linguistic research reveals profound diversity in how languages employ prosody, syntax, and semantics to mark focus, offering a window into language typology and evolution. At a neurocognitive level, focus processing is intimately linked to attention and prediction mechanisms, with neural correlates (e.g., activity in the superior temporal gyrus) being identified for intonational contours. Despite significant progress, an integrated understanding of focus across theoretical, experimental, and applied domains remains elusive.

title: Enhancing Brain Health: Physical, Cognitive, and Nutritional Interventions
summary: Brain health reflects the dynamic interplay of neural development, plasticity, and resilience across the lifespan. Emerging evidence shows that physical activity, cognitive engagement, and nutritional status each exert powerful, and often synergistic, effects on brain structure and function. These influences extend from early neurodevelopment through healthy ageing, and shape vulnerability to neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative conditions. At the same time, environmental exposures, genetic background, and lifestyle factors interact in complex ways that remain incompletely understood. Within clinical neuroscience, there is a growing need to clarify how targeted interventions in these domains can promote optimal nervous system development, preserve cognitive function, and mitigate disease risk. This Research Topic will integrate mechanistic, translational, and clinical research to delineate how physical, cognitive, and nutritional interventions can enhance brain health.

title: Virtual Bodies for Real Humans - Avatars, Sensations and Emotions
summary: Our bodies are fundamental to how we experience and interact with the physical world, and they shape the way our minds develop. The human brain develops together with the rest of the human body, adapting to its specific properties like size, weight or the resulting biomechanics. Virtual/extended reality (VR), on the other hand, allows us to instantly assume a virtual body (avatar) of any kind. While virtual bodies do not need to follow real-world physical, anatomical or biomechanical constraints, their users are humans whose brains are wired to represent human bodies. VR enables embodiment in entirely new forms—human, animal, robotic, or abstract—raising profound questions: How does our human sensorimotor experience shape interactions in non-human avatars? How can we create realistic sensations and emotional expressions for virtual bodies?

title: Music and the Brain: From Neural Mechanisms to Clinical Applications
summary: The field of music neuroscience explores how music engages complex brain networks, making it a uniquely powerful tool for investigating neural processes that underpin perception, action, emotion, prediction, and reward. Recent advances in neuroscience demonstrate that music activates widespread brain systems, from the auditory cortex to motor and reward networks, enabling the study of core principles such as neural entrainment, oscillatory timing, and predictive processing. Large-scale, multimodal studies have begun to illuminate how music can serve as both a model for basic brain function and as a pathway for understanding neurological and psychiatric disorders. Yet, critical gaps persist in linking circuit-level findings to clinically meaningful outcomes, elucidating moderators across development, and leveraging music as a precision tool for diagnosis and intervention.

AI in Human Neuroscience, Ethically Done: Neuroethical Risks, Safeguards, and Governance
summary: Artificial intelligence is revolutionizing human neuroscience, enabling unprecedented advances in brain imaging analysis, neural decoding, predictive modeling, and personalized neurological interventions. However, the rapid integration of AI into neuroscience research and clinical applications raises critical ethical concerns that remain inadequately addressed. These include privacy vulnerabilities with neural data, algorithmic bias in brain-based diagnostic tools, issues of informed consent in AI-driven neuroscience studies, and the potential misuse of neural information for non-medical purposes. As AI systems become increasingly sophisticated and widely deployed, there is an urgent need for comprehensive frameworks that balance scientific innovation with robust ethical safeguards. This Research Topic brings together neuroscientists, ethicists, technologists, and policymakers to advance the responsible integration of AI in human neuroscience.

title: The Future of Brain Imaging: Techniques and Applications
summary: Brain imaging technologies have been instrumental in advancing our understanding of neural structure, function, and connectivity. Established techniques such as MRI, fMRI, PET, and EEG have provided invaluable insights into brain organization and dynamics in both health and disease. However, the field is rapidly evolving with the emergence of innovative imaging modalities and methodological refinements. Next-generation approaches—including ultra-high field imaging, multimodal integration, real-time imaging, functional ultrasound, and AI-enhanced analysis pipelines—promise unprecedented spatial and temporal resolution. These advances are expanding the frontiers of what we can measure and understand about the human brain, while simultaneously presenting new challenges in data interpretation, standardization, and clinical translation. This Research Topic explores the current state and future trajectory of brain imaging science.

Leveraging edge AI enables decentralized, real-time computation that meets the demanding requirements of today's robotic applications.

title: The interplay between economic and biopsychosocial factors in brain health
summary: Financial well-being is a strong determinant of human. Individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds encounter a disproportionate amount of chronic stress, limited access to resources, and reduced opportunities for cognitive stimulation, all of which can profoundly influence brain development and functioning across the lifespan. At the same time, biological factors (e.g., genetic and biomarker-based risk factors), cognitive function and numerical abilities, and mental health variables like depression and anxiety, can influence an individual's ability to acquire and manage financial resources. There is likely a reciprocal relationship between financial well-being and the brain. Despite growing interest in this field, the bidirectional mechanisms linking economic factors to brain functioning, and health remain poorly understood.

Computational mechanisms of sensory and multisensory integration in perception and action
summary: While considerable progress has been made in mapping sensory and multisensory processing at behavioral and neural levels, key questions remain regarding the computational rules and neural implementations underlying integration. How does the brain weigh and combine inputs with varying reliability? At what stages and under what conditions are signals fused versus maintained separately? How do these processes differ between perception and action, and which neurobiological mechanisms are shared or distinct? This Research Topic aims to bring together interdisciplinary investigations that combine neurophysiology, psychophysics, computational modeling, and artificial intelligence to reveal new insights into the computational principles governing multisensory integration. By synthesizing experimental, theoretical, and applied approaches, we seek to clarify how the brain manages sensory uncertainties and coordinates perception with flexible, goal-directed action.

summary: The experience of stress is an inevitable part of human life, affecting individuals physically, emotionally, and psychologically. From brief tension-filled moments to chronic stress exposure, the resulting impact on the human brain is profound, influencing neural circuits and even altering brain function. Despite its potential detriments, stress also presents an opportunity for resilience—an adaptive response enabling individuals to maintain mental health despite adversity. This area of research is crucial for advancing our understanding of how resilience is cultivated and how stress can be managed effectively to prevent stress-related disorders. The field of human neuroscience offers valuable insights into the underlying biological mechanisms that govern stress responses and resilience building.

title: Resilience and Psychological Recovery in Times of Stress and Uncertainty: Pathways to Mental Health and Human Flourishing
summary: The field of psychological resilience and adaptation has gained increasing relevance in recent years as individuals and societies face persistent stressors ranging from global crises to personal hardships. Research has illuminated the complex interplay between biological, psychological, and social processes that underpin human responses to adversity. Despite an expanding body of evidence, questions remain about how people rebuild wellbeing after disruption, the mechanisms that sustain recovery, and the factors that distinguish mere survival from genuine flourishing. Emerging studies challenge traditional deficit-oriented frameworks and instead highlight dynamic models of growth, flexibility, and meaning-making. Yet, gaps persist in understanding how contextual, cultural, and temporal factors influence the trajectories of psychological recovery and personal development.

Advancing Critical Military Suicide Studies: Challenging Assumptions and Innovating Prevention
summary: Suicide among military servicemembers and veterans is a profound and persistent public health challenge, manifesting across national and cultural contexts. Despite systematic surveillance, targeted research, and significant resource allocation over the past two decades, suicide rates within military and veteran populations have increased or remained elevated in many Western countries. Historically, efforts have concentrated on the identification of risk and protective factors, the development of clinical interventions, and the implementation of broad institutional prevention strategies. While substantial advancements have been made in clinical, policy, and programmatic domains, a deep-seated paradox persists: investments in conventional prevention strategies have not consistently produced meaningful reductions in suicide deaths or been sufficiently responsive to the unique needs of the military and veteran community, highlighting gaps in our theoretical and practical approaches.

summary: Geriatric psychiatry sits at the intersection of neuroscience, psychology, and clinical medicine, addressing the complex mental health challenges that accompany aging. Older adults often present with multifactorial conditions, including depression, anxiety, cognitive decline, psychotic symptoms, medication effects, and sleep disruption, that rarely conform to a single explanatory level. Recent research highlights complex interactions among neurobiological changes, psychopathological presentations, psychopharmacological treatments, and psychosocial variables such as loneliness and autonomy. Despite growing evidence, clinical care models often remain fragmented, with limited integration between neuropsychological assessment, biological mechanisms, and treatment approaches. This integration gap underscores the need for a translational, multidisciplinary framework spanning the continuum from neuropsychological and neurobiological mechanisms to psychopathology and treatment in later life.

summary: Traumatic experiences are recognized as a significant risk factor for the development of substance-related and behavioral addictions in both adolescence and adulthood. Further research should extend current knowledge to different cultural contexts and promote the development or adaptation of culturally sensitive tools for investigating the trauma–addiction relationship. Embodied Approaches to Intervention and Research Design in Clinical Psychology: Integrating Body, Context, and Measurement
summary: Clinical psychology has long recognized that psychological distress and therapeutic change involve more than cognitive processes alone. Emotion regulation, symptom expression, trauma responses, and treatment outcomes are shaped by bodily states, autonomic function, interoceptive awareness, and the lived contexts in which clients exist. Yet clinical research methods can overlook these embodied dimensions. Treating physiological variability, posture, breath, circadian timing, and relational dynamics as clinically meaningful variables can bring further insight into treatment and management pathways. When embodied dimensions are not systematically incorporated into research design and measurement, this can limit the precision of assessment, weaken treatment specificity, and contribute to unexplained variance in clinical outcomes.

summary: Within the field of health psychology, there is growing recognition of the importance of psychosocial factors such as spirituality and religiousness (S/R) in shaping mental health outcomes. Despite a longstanding debate, recent evidence points toward both beneficial and adverse effects of S/R practices on psychological well-being. Some studies highlight how spiritual or religious engagement can provide individuals with meaning, purpose, and feelings of belonging, which serve as protective factors against mood disorders and psychological distress. Conversely, other research points to potentially negative consequences arising from rigid belief systems, religious struggles, or experiences of exclusion and existential doubt. The complex relationship between S/R and mental health is further complicated by cultural, contextual, and individual differences, underscoring the need for more nuanced and integrative research in this area.

title: (Re-)Theorizing the Psyche: Exploring Foundational Shifts in Psychological Science
summary: The replication crisis has exposed deep-seated tensions within psychological science. Beyond technical or procedural flaws, it has raised fundamental questions about the epistemic architecture and ontological assumptions of the discipline. While most responses have focused on methodological refinement, such as improved statistical tools, preregistration, or open science initiatives, these efforts often leave unexamined the more foundational question: what the replication crisis reveals about psychological theory and about the assumptions psychology makes about its object of inquiry, the “psyche” beyond technical procedure.

title: Ergonomics of Recovery: Enhancing Mental or Cognitive Workload Relief and Well-Being in Contemporary Workplaces
summary: The field of workplace ergonomics has expanded rapidly in response to the cognitive, emotional, and physical demands of contemporary work environments, particularly as organizations adopt digital and hybrid modalities. In this context, mental workload—often used interchangeably with cognitive workload—refers to the psychological demands placed on attention, memory, and executive control during task performance. Advances in technology have increased flexibility and connectivity but also intensified risks of mental workload accumulation, psychological strain, and blurred work-life boundaries. Prolonged digital exposure, multitasking, and reduced restorative breaks can undermine employee well-being and performance. These challenges highlight the need to translate ergonomic and human factors principles into practical strategies that foster cognitive recovery, inclusivity, and sustainable organizational effectiveness.

While attempts to pinpoint a central timekeeping hub continue, understanding time perception's involvement across various neurological and developmental disorders, such as autism or ADHD, remains essential. title: Unraveling the Neuropsychological Ground of Substance-Related and Non-Substance-Related Addictive Behaviors
summary: Modern neuropsychology views addiction as the behavioral consequence of neuroadaptation including notably maladaptive recalibration of the reward system from "liking" (hedonic pleasure) to "wanting" (compulsive craving), a breakdown in executive control and abnormal emotional processing. The state of the art in addiction neuropsychology has shifted from a simple "dopamine rush" theory to a complex neuro-circuitry model characterized by multiple structural and functional brain reorganization. Neuropsychology considers both the risk factors and the consequences of addictive behaviors, with an interest on recovery and the reversibility of neurobiological process. Based on the heterogeneity of profiles, the field is moving toward individual neuropsychological phenotyping, including cognitive, behavioral and emotional abilities, which would allow us to stratify patients and provide personalized and adapted care.

title: Brain Organization and Behavioral Asymmetries: From Sensory Processing to Cognition Across Species
summary: The two hemispheres of the brain are neither structurally nor functionally symmetrical, and these asymmetries are often reflected in behavior. For more than a century, it was a common but mistaken belief that lateralization was unique to the human brain. However, it is now well established that hemispheric asymmetries are fundamental components of sensory, cognitive, and motor systems across vertebrates and many invertebrates. Behavioral measures such as motor preferences and perceptual biases provide valuable tools for investigating these processes, reflecting links between observable behavior and neural organization. Evidence across taxa also suggests that hemispheric asymmetries may confer evolutionary advantages by enhancing neural efficiency and supporting perceptual, cognitive, and motor performance, with potential benefits for survival.

Recent advances in cognitive science and deep learning have shed light on consciousness theories, enhancing our understanding of potential AI sentience. How close are we to realizing sentient AI, and what moral implications would it imply?

title: Pushed to Choose: Motivational, Emotional, and Physiological Processes in Police Decision-Making
summary: Police decision-making often unfolds in emotionally charged, uncertain, and time-pressured environments. Officers are required to interpret ambiguous cues, regulate affect, assess risk, and act in ways that are lawful, proportionate, and operationally effective. Yet these decisions are not shaped by cognition alone. Emotional states, chronic occupational stress, fatigue, burnout, trauma exposure, moral strain, and psychological well-being can all influence attention, judgment, impulse control, communication, and post-incident recovery. At the same time, the consequences of police decisions extend beyond individual performance to public trust, procedural justice, use-of-force outcomes, and officers’ long-term mental health. A focused discussion of how emotional processes and well-being interact with police decision-making is therefore timely and necessary, both for psychological theory and for evidence-informed practice.

summary: Psychological science is at a crossroads. The last two decades has brought a range of fundamental issues into focus, including the replication crisis highlighted by large-scale community efforts such as the Open Science Collaboration, problems with representativeness and diversity emphasized by researchers such as Apicella, Norenzayan, and Henrich, and concerns regarding the very nature of the construction of theories raised by Oberauer and Lewandowsky; and van Rooij and Baggio, and more recent contributions by van Dongen and colleagues. At the same time, long-standing questions about explanation, evidence, and mind-world relations are now intersecting with rapid developments in cognitive science, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence. These converging trends highlight both the urgency and the opportunity for rigorous theoretical and philosophical work that can clarify, critique, and guide the future of psychology.

title: Developing Musical Expression, Communication, and Wellbeing
summary: Through music people express themselves, their ideas, thoughts and feelings. Music holds affordances for meaning making and communication that can be beneficial for health and wellbeing. Musical expression and communication have the potential to enhance people's sense of wellbeing; however, this does not happen automatically and can be particularly challenging for those studying or working within the music profession. title: Psychological Health and Safety at Work: A Systems-Level Approach to Psychosocial Risk, Organizational Context, and Employee Well-Being
summary: Psychological health and safety (PHS) has emerged as a critical priority in contemporary workplaces, reflecting growing recognition of psychosocial risks such as excessive workload, job insecurity, and poor organizational support. Frameworks such as the Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) model and psychosocial safety climate (PSC) highlight how work design, leadership, and human resource practices shape both risk and protective factors. Recent developments, including international standards such as ISO 45003, further underscore the need for integrated approaches to managing psychological health and safety. This Research Topic builds on this shift by examining how organizational systems create, sustain, or mitigate psychosocial risk and influence employee well-being.

summary: Immersive VR and XR now allow perceptual science to be conducted under rich, interactive conditions that approximate everyday sensorimotor engagement better than conventional screen-based paradigms. However, virtual worlds are not neutral containers: presence, embodiment, and agency can amplify attentional capture and reshape perceptual judgments, while device optics, latency, locomotion interfaces, and haptic realism can introduce systematic biases. As a result, findings obtained in virtual environments may diverge from classic laboratory outcomes in both magnitude and mechanism. summary: In recent years, the dialogue around Adultcentrism and its methodological derivation Bleak Pedagogy, formerly known as Black Pedagogy, has gained significant attention. These concepts offer pivotal frameworks for examining and enhancing children’s well-being and the quality of adult-child interactions, shedding light on educational relationships from a critical perspective. Adultcentrism (AD) is identified as a paradigm of thought where adults perceive children’s worlds and capacities from a biased adult-centric viewpoint, often evaluating youth abilities in relation to adult norms and expectations. This can lead to a misalignment between actual child needs and the intentions of well-meaning adults, influenced by societal pressures and personal biases.

Cortical Plasticity in Retinal Disease: Mechanisms of Reorganization following Vision Loss
summary: Retinal disease, whether caused by age-related macular degeneration, retinitis pigmentosa, inherited macular and cone–rod dystrophies, or diabetic retinopathy, was long thought to leave the visual cortex it deprives essentially silent. Over the past two decades, that view has been overturned: neurons formerly driven by the lesioned retina begin responding to stimulation from surrounding, intact regions, receptive-field properties shift, and measurable functional and structural remodeling emerges across the visual pathway. Understanding the mechanisms, limits, and behavioral consequences of this plasticity is now central to both basic visual neuroscience and the design of restorative and rehabilitative therapies.

summary: Traditional educational models often treat cognition and emotion as separate domains, overlooking their deeply interconnected relationship. Advances in neuropsychology and cognitive neuroscience have shown that this symbiosis arises from dynamic interactions within corticolimbic circuits, principally involving executive functioning (prefrontal cortex), emotional regulation (amygdala), and working memory (hippocampus). Recently, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), with its capabilities in generating personalized content, can reshape intertwined processes of cognitive and emotional learning. By leveraging neuroscience methodologies like EEG, fNRI and neurofeedback, GenAI can establish real-time feedback loops using physiological markers (e.g., amygdala reactivity) to reinforce cognition-emotion development.

title: Homo Aquaticus: New Frontiers in Living and Working in the Ocean
summary: The ocean plays a critical role in the well-being of all humans on the planet, yet in many ways, we are still just at the beginning stages of ocean exploration. This gap in our understanding is particularly salient in the context of human presence within (as opposed to, on the surface of) the sea. Recent advances in several areas of marine research and technology as well as in the social sciences have the potential to re-envision how we work within the ocean, ranging from telepresence via robots to direct observation via brief visits using crewed submersibles to living on the seafloor using saturation diving. Yet the full potential of these methods to fully engage the non-scientific public requires a new paradigm for how Western societies live and work as part of the ocean, ideas envisaged using cutting-edge methods of storytelling such as film and serious games, and informed by multiple non-Western cultures.

summary: The relationship between physical activity and mental health has long been recognized; however, it has only been in recent decades that cognitive neuroscience has begun to elucidate the underlying neural mechanisms. Converging evidence from neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and neurochemical studies indicates that exercise induces profound changes in brain structure and function. These biological processes are increasingly understood to mediate the beneficial effects of physical activity on mood, cognitive function, and resilience to psychological stress. However, despite this progress, the cognitive neuroscience of exercise remains an underexplored frontier, with the precise mechanisms through which physical activity promotes mental health still incompletely understood.

summary: Elite soccer performance has traditionally been examined through physical, technical, and tactical metrics. At the same time, advances in soccer analytics and artificial intelligence have expanded the capacity to quantify match behavior and physiological responses. Despite these developments, psychological determinants are often examined in isolation, while data-driven performance models rarely integrate psychological constructs in a systematic and ecologically valid manner.

Beyond motor and cognitive outcomes, successful XR-based rehabilitation critically depends on psychological factors such as motivation, engagement, emotional regulation, and perceived experience. At the same time, XR systems enable multimodal data acquisition, including behavioral metrics and neurophysiological signals such as EEG and MRI, offering unprecedented opportunities for objective, continuous, and ecologically valid assessment of psychological, behavioral, and physiological processes. However, the rapid technological development has outpaced the establishment of standardized, quantitative measures capable of capturing both subjective psychological processes and their underlying neural and physiological correlates within rehabilitation contexts.

summary: The boundaries between work and non-work life have never been more blurred. As hybrid arrangements consolidate as the dominant model in knowledge-intensive sectors, employees increasingly move between professional and personal domains — often within the same physical space. While hybrid work offers autonomy and flexibility, growing evidence suggests it also reshapes the psychological mechanisms through which employees disengage from work, recover from daily demands, and protect their well-being. title: Thriving While Work Is Rewritten: Innovation and Sustainable Work in the Adjacent Possible
summary: Work is being rewritten on several fronts at once, by technological developments such as digitalisation and generative AI, by organisational changes such as algorithmic management and hybrid work, and by broader societal pressures including sustainability demands and demographic change. These changes do not merely introduce new tools or procedures; they reshape expectations, relationships, employment lifecycles, opportunities, and constraints within organisations. This Research Topic adopts the lens of the adjacent possible to explore how innovation in work design, organisational processes, and structures unfolds from what already exists, opening new pathways for action, adaptation, and development while also generating new tensions, risks, and inequalities. At the centre of the Topic is the question of thriving, whether and under what conditions people and organisations can flourish rather than merely cope as work is reconfigured.

This Research Topic aims to explore the psychoeducational implications of affective-sexual education from early childhood to university, addressing its role in promoting holistic development and equipping young people with the tools to navigate complex social and emotional landscapes.

title: Influenza Call For Papers
summary: CALL FOR PAPERS Influenza PLOS ONE Submit to this PLOS ONE call for papers to help expand the global knowledge on influenza. Submission deadline, April 09, 2021. This call for papers is closed. Submit to PLOS ONE Apr 9 2021 SCOPE Influenza is an important cause of death and morbidity globally. While vaccination is the best way to prevent influenza virus infection, other pharmaceutical and non-pharmaceutical strategies can prevent or mitigate the impact of influenza on individuals and the spread within populations. Influenza viruses are continually evolving, posing challenges to vaccination strategies and vaccine development. This PLOS ONE call for papers aims to create a collection of research articles that focuses on influenza prevention on every level. We welcome submissions reporting in vitro , translational, and clinical studies; disease and immunity modelling; as well as new approaches to influenza prevention.
